result:
The house speaks in the dark, but not in words. It speaks in the slow tick of a pipe cooling in the kitchen wall, in the almost-imperceptible groan of the joists under the weight of a mattress no one is sleeping on. There is a particular creak in the hallway that means the oak is contracting by a fraction of a millimeter, the wood remembering it was once a tree that held a specific amount of rain in its rings.

I think about this more than I should. About how every building is a compressed history of weather. The plaster holds the damp of the year it was hung. The nails were forged in a summer so distant it belongs to a different species of human. The floorboards still have the ghost-geometry of every footstep that ever pressed down and released, thousands of small surrenders to gravity accumulated into a landscape of wear.

And then the sound that makes me press my ear to the wall at 2 a.m., the one that isn't a pipe or a joist but something lower, structural, like the house is exhaling a long-held sentence it forgot how to finish. The whole frame shifting two degrees from where the sun left it this afternoon. A settling. A decision. The building choosing a new arrangement of its own bones while I lie awake in it, held.

It is not loneliness. It is the opposite of loneliness, actually. It is the specific, quiet agreement between a person and a structure that says: *I will hold you tonight. You do not have to hold anything back.*

And the house, being made of wood and iron and the particular silence of a Tuesday, holds me.
